headline: 7 common vulnerabilities found in AI-generated code with an open-source scanner
summary: A new static analysis tool identifies 7 specific vulnerability patterns in code produced by AI assistants like Copilot, often due to AI optimizing for 'plausible examples' over production safety.
details: Developers using AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot or Claude Code might unknowingly ship specific bugs. A new static analysis tool, ai-vuln-scan, was built to identify these unique vulnerability patterns.

The core issue is that AI assistants optimize for 'plausible, runnable examples' rather than production-ready, secure code. This often leads to omissions of crucial security practices unless explicitly prompted.
Seven distinct patterns were identified, including hardcoded secrets in placeholder form, unparameterized query construction, and shell commands built via string interpolation.
Other patterns involve permissive default configurations, use of weak cryptographic primitives, inconsistent authorization across similar routes, and verbose error responses leaking internal details.
These findings are documented in the public AI Vulnerability Pattern Catalog, and the ai-vuln-scan tool is open-source, allowing developers to systematically catch these predictable classes of bugs.

Seven distinct patterns were identified, including hardcoded secrets in placeholder form, unparameterized query construction, and shell commands built via string interpolation.

Other patterns involve permissive default configurations, use of weak cryptographic primitives, inconsistent authorization across similar routes, and verbose error responses leaking internal details.

These findings are documented in the public AI Vulnerability Pattern Catalog, and the ai-vuln-scan tool is open-source, allowing developers to systematically catch these predictable classes of bugs.

headline_marked: [[Mexican student invents acoustic fire extinguisher]] that puts out flames with sound in seconds
headline: Mexican student invents acoustic fire extinguisher that puts out flames with sound in seconds
summary: 16-year-old Ángela Karime Venegas Hernández developed "Vortex Tech," a device using 30 pulses per second of sound to extinguish fires on various materials without water or chemicals.
details: 16-year-old Ángela Karime Venegas Hernández from Mexico has developed an acoustic fire extinguisher. Her invention, named 'Vortex Tech,' uses sound waves to put out fires in seconds, offering a novel approach to fire safety.

The device operates with a 12-volt battery, a frequency generator, and a speaker that emits 30 pulses per second. These vibrations effectively push oxygen away from the flames, causing the fire to extinguish in just five to eight seconds.

Extensively tested over 100 times, Vortex Tech has proven effective on various types of fires, including wood, flammable liquids, cooking grease, and electronic equipment. It offers a clean solution, leaving no residue and posing no harm to the user or environment.

What began as a school experiment is now set to represent Mexico at an international fair. Ángela will present her innovative method of combating one of humanity's oldest dangers to a global audience.
